title: Effects of Illuminance and Correlated Color Temperature on Daytime Cognitive Performance, Subjective Mood, and Alertness in Healthy Adults
research_question: This study investigated the impact of indoor illuminance and correlated color temperature (CCT) on healthy adults' cognitive performance, subjective mood, and alertness during daytime office hours and differences in time-of-day effects. The study also aimed to explore whether light effects could be understood in terms of affective state elicited by light exposure.

participants.description: Sixty healthy adults (mean age = 22.28 ± 0.17 years, range 18-25) from Guangzhou, China. All were right-handed, in good physical and psychological health (GHQ-20), had normal/corrected-to-normal vision, regular sleep/wake patterns (MEQ), and no sleep problems (PSQI > 7) or affective disorders (BDI-II). Exclusion criteria included smoking, daily alcohol/caffeine, medication/drug use, BMI outside 18.5-23.9, and shift work/transmeridional flights in the past 2 months.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through Internet sites at local universities in Guangzhou, China.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A simulated, windowless office (4.1m x 3.3m x 2.9m) with four workstations separated by ground-glass panels. Air temperature (25°C) and humidity (40%-60%) were controlled. Lighting conditions were created using nine ceiling-mounted LED luminaires (Philips T8-20 W/865 for 6500K cool white; T8-20 W/830 for 3000K warm white). Illuminance was varied by changing the number of LED tubes (three for 1200 lx, one for 200 lx).

findings.mechanism: Participants had more correct responses in the bright light exposure.

findings.antecedent: Illuminance x CCT x Type of word x Time of day interaction (high cool light, afternoon, neutral words)
findings.mechanism: Participants performed best (fastest RT) in high cool light when recognizing neutral words in the afternoon.
findings.quote: The RT results showed a four-way interaction among illuminance, color temperature, type of word, and time of day, F(2,112) = 4.74, p = .011, d = 0.59 (Table 8). Participants performed best in the high cool light as compared with other light exposures, but only when recognizing neutral words in the afternoon rather than in the morning, t(33) = 2.80, p = .009, d = 0.87.

findings.mechanism: Participants performed better (faster RT) in low cool than low warm light. Under cool light, RTs were shorter in bright than dim light.
findings.quote: an interaction between illuminance and color temperature, F(1,56) = 5.21, p = .026, d = 0.63 (Table 8). mechanisms: Arousal theories: High illuminance may increase mental arousal, enhancing easy cognitive performance.
Mood-congruence effect: Participants' positive mood may facilitate the judgment of positive facial expressions.
Emotional meaning of lighting: Indoor lighting conditions can communicate different emotional meanings to humans.
Affective state not a mediator: Positive affect did not mediate the relationship between lighting conditions and cognitive performance.
moderators: Type of word (positive, neutral, negative for long-term memory)
Facial emotions (happy, fearful, neutral for facial expression judgment)
implementation_implications: Exposure to bright light is effective for enhancing alertness, mood, and maintaining a positive attitude toward work during daytime office hours.
LED lighting systems, with superior light output, lower power consumption, and longer usable lifetime, are ideal for offices and school buildings.
Low warm light, while eliciting positive mood and comfort, contributes little to cognitive performance improvement and may not be optimal for daytime office settings.

limitations: A large percentage of the sample consisted of females, which may limit generalizability regarding gender differences.
Only two levels of illuminance and CCT were employed, and a limited set of cognitive tasks were used, limiting the scope for determining optimal lighting characteristics.
Individual differences in lighting preference were not measured, which could influence subjective evaluations and objective performance.
Findings were obtained under strictly controlled laboratory conditions of relatively brief duration, limiting generalizability to actual work settings.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of Illuminance and Correlated Color Temperature on Daytime Cognitive Performance, Subjective Mood, and Alertness in Healthy Adults
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This study investigated the impact of indoor illuminance and correlated color temperature (CCT) on healthy adults’ cognitive performance, subjective mood, and alertness during daytime office hours and differences in time-of-day effects. A 2(illuminance) × 2(CCT) × 2(morning vs. afternoon) mixed design ( N = 60) was employed. Participants felt less sleepy in the bright light exposure. The low “cool” lighting induced the least positive mood. The effects of illuminance and CCT on subjective feelings were not time-of-day dependent. The results demonstrated the slowest responses in inhibition, working memory, and recognition of facial expression tasks in the low “warm” lighting. The effect on long-term memory was most pronounced under the high “cool” light exposure, but only in the afternoon for recognition of neutral words. The findings suggest that future research on good indoor lighting should consider illuminance levels and CCT as well as other variables to optimize lighting effects during regular daytime hours.
